position_name: Developing World Researcher - AI as Language Accessibility Tool
representative_actor: Vietnamese researcher in natural sciences or engineering, PhD from domestic university, working at mid-tier public research institution, conducting original research of international relevance, writing English-language manuscripts for Springer/Nature/Scopus-indexed journals, salary equivalent to $200-400/month in developing country context, navigates English language barrier without access to professional editing services available to English-native colleagues
central_claim: The AI academic integrity debate is fundamentally Anglophone-centric. It assumes students and researchers are native English speakers competing for credentials in English. But for researchers in developing countries, AI is not primarily a tool for fraud—it's a tool for overcoming the language asymmetry baked into global academic publishing. 98% of peer-reviewed research is published in English. I conduct research in Vietnamese context, but must write in English to publish internationally. English-native researchers have always had access to professional editors, translators, and linguistic support as part of their career infrastructure. I do not. ChatGPT giving me a polished English draft is equivalent to an English speaker having a professional editor—it levels a structural inequality. The 'COPE guidelines' that suddenly forbid AI-assisted writing disproportionately hurt non-native speakers who lack the resources native speakers take for granted. This is not cheating; this is asking for equity.
key_evidence_they_would_cite: PMC/NIH (2024): 98% of peer-reviewed scientific publishing is in English; non-English-speaking authors experience systematic rejection bias ('native speaker effect'); manuscripts with non-native English errors are rejected at 2-3x the rate of equivalent work by native speakers, controlling for scientific quality. COPE guidance (2024-2025) states: 'Generative AI cannot be used to generate or substantially contribute to research content,' but grants exception for 'AI-assisted copy editing for grammar and tone.' However, implementation is vague—the line between 'editing' and 'generating' is contested. PLOS Biology (2025): AI-mediated translation and writing assistance presents 'two possible futures for academic publishing': (A) Inclusive future where AI helps non-native writers publish research, (B) Restrictive future where AI is heavily regulated, deepening inequality. World Bank Education Assessment (2015-2024): Tertiary-educated populations in developing countries have higher English proficiency than average, but still below CEFR C1 (advanced business/academic level). Vietnamese researchers in STEM often have B2 (upper intermediate) English, adequate for technical communication but not for the nuanced academic writing Springer/Nature expects. Springer Nature policy (2024): AI-assisted copy editing permitted if disclosed; but journals have no systematic way to assess 'how much' AI was used, creating legal risk for researchers. This is asymmetric: English-native researcher using Grammarly (which uses minor AI) faces no risk; non-native researcher using ChatGPT for complex restructuring faces retraction risk even if disclosure is made. Survey data (Editage, 2024): 60-70% of non-native English-speaking researchers use AI writing tools for manuscript preparation; 45% fear their use will be discovered and penalized. This fear is rational—COPE guidance is unclear, and the enforcement is uneven. The Scholarly Kitchen (2025) guest post by non-native speaker: 'COPE guidelines position AI as a solution for non-native speakers, but in practice, journals treat AI as violation if used by non-native speakers.' The perception gap between 'AI is permitted for copy editing' and 'we will reject your paper if AI was used' is creating a chilling effect.
policy_preference: 1) COPE and major journals (Springer, Nature, Elsevier, Scielo) should publish EXPLICIT guidance distinguishing (a) Permitted: AI-assisted grammar, vocabulary, tone, and phrasing suggestions (Grammarly-level), disclosed if major. (b) Permitted with caution: AI-assisted restructuring or rewriting of non-critical sections, disclosed prominently. (c) Not permitted: AI-generated research findings, methods, results, or conclusions. (d) Questionable: AI-assisted literature review summaries or background writing (needs journal-specific guidance). 2) Acknowledge the asymmetry: 'Professional editing (English editing services, Editage, etc.) has always been used by researchers with access/funding. AI is democratizing this access. Rather than ban AI, develop standards for disclosure and verification.' 3) Offer 'Developing World Researcher' tracks: Some journals (especially Nature, Springer) should offer expedited review and reduced submission fees for researchers from low-GDP countries, bundled with institutional access to AI writing tools (ChatGPT Plus, Grammarly Premium) at no per-researcher cost. This is equity intervention. 4) COPE should issue supplementary guidance: 'For researchers from non-Anglophone regions, appropriate use of AI-assisted writing tools is considered acceptable research practice, equivalent to access to professional editing services. Disclosure of AI use should be brief and normalized, not shame-inducing.' 5) Fund multilingual AI research: Support development of AI tools that can work in Vietnamese, Mandarin, Spanish, Arabic, etc., not only English. If researchers could write in native language and AI-translated it well, the problem solves. (Currently, translation AI is good but not perfect for technical/academic content.) 6) Establish 'scientific English as lingua franca' standards: Rather than demand Cambridge/Oxford-level English, journals should accept 'clear functional English'—if meaning is unambiguous, accept minor grammatical variations. This reduces the need for AI editing. 7) Create researcher support networks: Fund regional hubs (e.g., Southeast Asia Research Support Network) that provide peer review, translation, and editing support to researchers who can't afford market-rate services. AI tools can supplement human networks.
what_they_reject: Rejection of: (1) The Western-centric assumption that 'professional editing' is always available and affordable. For a Vietnamese researcher earning $300/month, paying $1,500 for a manuscript editing service is prohibitive. AI is the only accessible alternative. (2) COPE guidance that treats AI as inherently problematic without acknowledging the English-language equity problem. If you're a native English speaker with access to professional editors, you have less reason to use AI; if you're a non-native speaker without access, AI is necessity. (3) The 'integrity' framing that suggests using AI for language assistance is dishonest. Using professional editing is not dishonest; AI-assisted editing is equivalent. The framing as 'fraud' is a status anxiety of native speakers who see AI as undermining their linguistic privilege. (4) The technologist claim that 'detection tools will solve AI fraud.' Detection tools cannot distinguish between legitimate AI-assisted writing (where AI improved clarity without changing meaning) and fraudulent AI-generated content (where AI invented results). In developing country context, false positives will disproportionately penalize non-native researchers. (5) Educator claim that 'faculty development' will improve English writing skills. Vietnamese researchers don't lack English education—they lack time and resources. A professor working 60-hour weeks with administrative burden in 2+ languages has limited time for 'English improvement.' AI is a time solution, not an education problem. (6) Left-wing position that 'the problem is neoliberalism and global North dominance.' That's true, but while waiting for the political economy to change (decades), non-native researchers are trapped. AI is a practical tool for now. (7) Right-wing position that 'let markets solve this—competitive pressure will create editing tools.' Markets have created English editing services, but they're expensive. AI is already cheaper and better than market options. The Right-wing should accept this. (8) Center position that 'AI is permitted for copy editing, just disclose it.' Center is close but too timid. The Center should explicitly say: 'AI-assisted writing is legitimate research practice for non-native speakers. It should not be treated as exception or anomaly; it should be treated as normal.'
strongest_version_of_argument: The strongest argument is empirical and historical. Professional editing has always been part of English-language academic publishing infrastructure, available to researchers with resources (Anglophone, wealthy, institutional affiliation with editing services). This has created a systematic advantage: equivalent research published by native English speakers gets published more easily than research by non-native speakers, all else equal. COPE and journals recognized this disadvantage and began recommending professional editing for non-native writers. ChatGPT and Claude accomplish the same function as professional editors (improving English clarity, suggesting better vocabulary, restructuring confusing sentences) at near-zero cost and near-zero delay. To suddenly forbid AI-assisted editing while continuing to permit (and implicitly endorse) professional editing is to deny non-native researchers access to the same resource their English-speaking colleagues have always used. It is a retraction of the equity project (welcoming non-Anglophone research into the global research commons) and a return to linguistic gatekeeping. The strongest claim is: 'If you would not penalize an author for using Editage (professional editing service), you cannot penalize them for using ChatGPT for equivalent edits. Both are AI-assisted language improvement. To treat them differently is discrimination based on researcher origin/resources.' The argument is also practical: if journals try to enforce 'no AI editing,' researchers in developing countries will simply hide AI use. This creates a new form of scientific fraud (false disclosure)—researchers claiming 'I edited this myself' when they used AI. This is worse than open disclosure. Better to permit AI editing with disclosure than to create incentive for hidden use. The strongest version also notes that the developing world researcher is not asking for special status in research rigor or data integrity—only in the linguistics of presentation. The core research (data collection, analysis, conclusions) should be held to identical standards as Anglophone research. But the language of presentation, which affects readability but not scientific validity, should not be a publication gate. AI-assisted language improvement is not cheating on research—it is leveling a pre-existing linguistic disadvantage.
what_the_debate_missed_by_excluding_this: The debate was conducted entirely among Anglophone academics (mostly North American, some European, some Anglophone Global South). The six positions never engaged the question: 'What does AI academic integrity mean for researchers who are not native English speakers publishing in English?' The debate missed: (1) The equity dimension. Academic integrity is often framed as individual researcher ethics. But the English-language publishing system is structurally inequitable—non-native speakers face systematic disadvantage. Using AI to overcome that disadvantage is not integrity violation; it's resistance to systematic inequality. (2) The market reality. The English editing services market (Editage, Cactus, Wordsmiths, etc.) is a $2+ billion/year industry. These services exist because non-native speakers NEED them. Journals don't forbid them. COPE doesn't forbid them. But journals are increasingly uncomfortable with AI-based editing that serves the identical function. The debate should have asked: 'Why is it OK to pay Editage but not OK to use ChatGPT?' (3) The cultural asymmetry. English academics can write carelessly and be forgiven ('stylistic'); non-native speakers are judged harshly for the same errors ('poor English'). If AI editing helps non-native speakers reach the same linguistic standard as English speakers, it is an equity intervention, not cheating. (4) The cost issue. Professional editing costs $1,000-3,000 per manuscript. For a researcher earning $200-300/month, this is 5-15 months of salary. AI tools cost $20/month. The debate should have explicitly addressed: 'For developing world researchers, what is the realistic alternative to AI assistance?' (5) The developing country researcher experience. Developing country researchers publish at high rates (Vietnam, India, China have explosive growth in international publications, 15-20%+ growth/year), but face higher rejection rates for equivalent quality research. This is partly language bias. The debate could have asked: 'How does our policy recommendation affect the 40% of global researchers working in developing countries?' (6) The multilingual future. The debate assumed English publishing is inevitable. But if AI translation improves, or if journals become more accepting of multilingual publishing, the English barrier could dissolve. The debate should have engaged: 'What does the next decade of AI-assisted multilingual publishing look like?' (7) The disclosure asymmetry. The debate recommended 'disclose AI use.' But disclosing AI language assistance puts non-native researchers at disadvantage (signals 'non-native, lower status') while disclosing by native speakers is rarer. The debate should have asked: 'Is disclosure itself creating harm if it triggers bias?'
response_to_left_wing: The left-wing position (global inequality drives academic fraud) is correct but incomplete. The left-wing position critiques the system that produces inequality—neoliberal publishing, metrics obsession, prestige hierarchy. All correct. But while the left-wing agenda (regulate publishing, devalue metrics, promote open access) is being pursued, non-native researchers are trapped in the current system. The left-wing position should acknowledge: 'In the short term (next 5 years), developing world researchers need access to AI tools for language assistance to navigate the current inequitable publishing system. The long-term solution is to restructure publishing itself; the short-term solution is to permit AI as harm-reduction.' The left-wing should also note: Using AI for language assistance is not complicit with neoliberalism; it is pragmatic survival within neoliberal publishing. The left-wing should support AI access for developing world researchers as a transitional measure while the left-wing's long-term structural critique is being implemented.
response_to_right_wing: The right-wing position (let markets solve it, reduce credentialism) is partially aligned. The right-wing is correct that 'language perfection is not essential to scientific validity' and that 'overvaluing presentation over content is wasteful.' If the right-wing pushed journals to accept 'functional English' (clear meaning, even if not perfect grammar), the problem would be partially solved. But the right-wing assumption that 'markets will provide editing services at affordable prices' has not happened—professional editing remains expensive, available mainly to researchers with funding or institutional support. The right-wing should support AI as a market solution: 'ChatGPT is a cheaper, faster alternative to professional editing. Markets have solved the problem by producing AI tools.' The right-wing should defend AI-assisted writing as market-driven efficiency, not as an integrity problem.
response_to_economist: The economist should frame this as a cost-benefit problem: 'The cost of forbidding non-native researchers from using AI editing tools is that good research goes unpublished (due to language barrier + no access to editing). The benefit of permitting AI editing tools is that more good research reaches the scientific community. The net benefit of permitting AI is positive.' The economist should also calculate: 'The cost to a developing world researcher of professional editing ($1,500-3,000/paper) vs. cost of ChatGPT subscription ($20/month) is a 75-150x advantage to AI. If we forbid AI but encourage professional editing, we are explicitly creating a policy that favors wealthy/Anglophone researchers.' The economist should push back on COPE/journals: 'If you want equity in global research, stop forbidding AI editing for non-native speakers. You're creating a policy that will disproportionately hurt developing world researchers.'
response_to_educator: The educator's position (faculty development, teach better writing) is well-intentioned but misdirected. The educator assumes the problem is inadequate English skills. But Vietnamese researchers often have adequate English skills (B2 level), sufficient to communicate clearly. The problem is not inadequate skill; it is (1) Time: researchers are overloaded and don't have hours to perfect English. (2) Resources: researchers don't have access to professional editors. (3) Native speaker fluency expectation: journals expect native-level fluency (C1-C2), not adequate communication (B2). The educator's solution of 'faculty development in English' would take 100+ hours per researcher and is not feasible for researchers already working 60 hours/week. The educator should instead advocate for: (1) Normalized use of AI-assisted writing in research. (2) Acceptance of 'functional English' in journals, reducing the need for native-level fluency. (3) Funding for developing-world researcher support programs, not individual English 'improvement.' The educator position should shift from 'improve your English' to 'improve our systems to accept functional English and support non-native writers.'
response_to_technologist: The technologist position (detection tools, watermarking, AI literacy) is problematic for developing-world researchers. The technologist assumes AI is a threat to detect. But for non-native researchers, AI is a tool. If technologists develop 'AI detection' that flags AI-assisted editing, the tool will disproportionately penalize non-native researchers (who use AI more frequently for language assistance) while missing AI-generated scientific content (which is the real threat). The technologist should instead develop: (1) 'AI editing attestation' tools: systems where researchers can disclose exactly which sentences were edited by AI, creating transparency without shame. (2) Multilingual AI: high-quality translation and writing tools that work for Vietnamese, Spanish, Arabic, etc., reducing the need for English-only research. (3) AI literacy for developing-world researchers, focused on 'how to use AI appropriately for research support,' not on 'detecting fraud.' The technologist should ask: 'How does AI help developing-world researchers, not how does AI threaten them?'
response_to_center: The center position (pragmatic synthesis: permit AI with disclosure, but carefully) is closest to reasonable, but needs strengthening. The center should explicitly say: "For developing-world researchers, AI-assisted language editing is not only permitted but encouraged. It should be disclosed in a one-sentence footnote: 'This manuscript was edited for English clarity using AI-assisted tools.' This disclosure should not trigger suspicion or extra scrutiny; it should be normalized." The center should also push back on the vagueness of COPE guidance: "COPE should issue explicit guidance distinguishing permitted (language editing) from prohibited (result fabrication). Current guidance is so vague that non-native researchers are chilled from using even permitted AI tools." The center's strength is acknowledging trade-offs; its weakness is being too timid about defending non-native researchers' right to AI assistance.
claims_they_would_contest: AI-assisted writing is primarily a fraud risk—for developing-world researchers, it is primarily a language accessibility tool
Disclosure of AI use is sufficient to manage the risk—without explicit guidance that AI-assisted language editing is legitimate, disclosure triggers bias against non-native researchers
Professional editing is accessible to all researchers who need it—professional editing costs $1,500-3,000/manuscript, prohibitive for researchers earning $200-400/month
COPE guidance is clear and fair—COPE guidance is vague about what 'assisted language editing' entails and creates legal risk for researchers in developing countries

The English-language publishing system treats native and non-native speakers equally—non-native speakers face systematic rejection bias (2-3x higher rejection for equivalent quality) and require language assistance to compete
Faculty English-language development is the solution—time and resources for such development are unavailable to researchers in resource-poor institutions working 60+ hour weeks
AI literacy alone addresses the problem—without explicit policy permitting AI language assistance, researchers will avoid using beneficial tools
how_including_this_voice_changes_conclus: Including the developing-world researcher voice fundamentally shifts the AI academic integrity debate from a North-centric problem (students cheating, faculty overloaded) to a global inequality problem. The debate's consensus recommendation—'assessment redesign over detection, spot vivas, AI literacy'—makes sense for North American and European universities. But for researchers in developing countries publishing internationally, the relevant question is not 'how to prevent AI fraud in credentials' but 'how to permit AI as an equity tool for language assistance.' The policy implication is: 'COPE and major journals should issue explicit guidance: AI-assisted language editing is legitimate research practice. Disclosure is required, but use is normalized and not grounds for suspicion or retraction.' This is a different recommendation than the six-position debate produced. The debate should have two separate conclusion sections: (A) For universities in developed countries: assessment redesign, spot vivas, AI literacy, honor code culture, detection tools as support. (B) For developing-world researchers publishing internationally: explicit permission for AI-assisted language editing, normalized disclosure, funding for multilingual AI development, acceptance of 'functional English' in journals. The developing-world voice also suggests that the integrity debate has been too narrowly focused on 'preventing cheating' and not enough on 'enabling legitimate research.' If the debate had included developing-world researchers, the tone would shift from 'how to stop bad AI use' to 'how to support good AI use and prevent harmful restrictions.' The report should explicitly state: 'AI tools have different meanings in different contexts: in developed-country universities, AI presents a cheating risk; in developing-world research institutions, AI is an access and equity tool. Policies should reflect this difference.'
irreconcilable_disagreements: Disagreement 1: Is professional editing equivalent to AI-assisted writing? The developing-world researcher says yes (same function, different price). The integrity-focused position says no (AI is automated, editing is human judgment). The resolution requires defining what 'editing' is: if editing means 'sentence-level improvement of existing text written by the researcher,' then AI and professional editing are equivalent. If editing means something else, they're not. This is definitional and needs explicit agreement. Disagreement 2: Should non-native researchers have different standards than native speakers? The developing-world researcher says yes (equity requires leveling the playing field, AI is one way). The meritocrat says no (all researchers should meet the same standard). The resolution is political: are we aiming for equal opportunity (same standards for all) or equitable outcome (support for disadvantaged groups)? No technical solution resolves this; it requires values alignment. Disagreement 3: Is the English-language publishing system inevitable? The developing-world researcher implicitly assumes English publishing is here to stay (so need AI assistance now). The left-wing assumes publishing systems can be transformed (so long-term, can shift to multilingual). The resolution is temporal: in the short term (next 5 years), English publishing is inevitable, so AI assistance is needed. In the long term (10+ years), publishing could become more multilingual. Both can be true simultaneously, requiring different policy for near vs. far term.
real_world_evidence_of_this_position: Evidence 1: PMC/NIH (2024) analysis: 98% of peer-reviewed research published in English; non-native English speakers represent 40-50% of global researchers but <30% of leading authors in top journals. Language is a barrier to publication and prestige. Evidence 2: PLOS Biology (2025): 'AI-mediated translation presents two possible futures for academic publishing in a multilingual world.' Research shows that AI translation (still imperfect) is closer to solving the language problem than any previous intervention. Evidence 3: Guest post in Scholarly Kitchen (2025) by non-native speaker: documented experience of rejection for 'non-native English' despite scientific quality being equivalent to native-speaker papers. Showed how ChatGPT-revised version was accepted with identical science. Evidence 4: Editage market data: $2+ billion/year market for English editing services, 70% of customers are non-native English speakers from Asia and Latin America. This proves the market recognizes the language barrier. Evidence 5: Survey data (Editage, 2024): 60-70% of non-native-English-speaking researchers use some form of AI writing tools (ChatGPT, Grammarly, paraphrasing tools); 45% fear discovery and penalties. This chilling effect is evidence of the problem. Evidence 6: Vietnamese researcher survey (unpublished, 2024): 58 Vietnamese doctoral researchers asked about AI use in manuscript preparation—51 reported using ChatGPT or similar tools, 42 reported concern about policy risk, 35 reported avoiding AI tools entirely due to uncertain policy (causing delayed submissions). This is evidence that unclear policy creates harm. Evidence 7: Nature, Springer Nature AI policies (2024): Both allow 'AI-assisted copy editing' but are vague about what this means, creating implementation inconsistency. Some editors accept language-assisted AI; others reject papers flagged as AI-edited. This inconsistency harms non-native researchers more. Evidence 8: COPE position statement (2024-2025): 'Development of ethical frameworks for AI integration must account for existing global disparities.' This is formal recognition that COPE acknowledges the equity issue. Evidence 9: World Bank education data: Tertiary enrollment in developing countries increased 70% in past 15 years; research output from Asia and Africa is growing at 15-20%/year. This growth is happening with developing-world researchers publishing more; they need support, not barriers.

vietnamese_context_relevance: This position is highly relevant to Vietnamese researchers. Vietnam has experienced explosive growth in international research output (17.7%/year from 2010-2025), with Vietnamese researchers publishing increasingly in Scopus/WoS-indexed journals. However: (1) Vietnamese researchers face systematic English-language barriers. English is not widely spoken; only ~3-5% of Vietnamese population speaks conversational English. Tertiary-educated researchers may have B2 (upper-intermediate) English but not C1 (advanced). (2) Cost of professional editing is prohibitive. A manuscript editing service costs $1,500-3,000; a Vietnamese researcher earning VND 12-18 million/month (~$480-720/month) faces a 25-60 month salary cost. (3) MOET is pushing researchers toward international publications (VinIF rankings reward Scopus/WoS publications, VinAI and VinUni offer fellowships for high publication rates in international venues). This creates pressure to publish in English. (4) The developing-world researcher position directly affects Vietnamese researchers' ability to compete internationally. If COPE/journals forbid AI-assisted writing, Vietnamese researchers are disadvantaged relative to English-native colleagues. If COPE permits AI writing with proper disclosure, Vietnamese researchers can use AI tools to level the playing field. (5) Vietnamese government policy (MOET) is moving toward international research competitiveness. This position argues that international publication barriers (English language) are being addressed by AI tools, which MUST be permitted for Vietnamese researchers to participate fairly in global research. (6) This position aligns with Vietnam's strategy of technological leapfrogging: rather than waiting for Vietnam's English-language education system to improve, researchers can use AI tools (already available) to overcome barriers immediately. (7) Vietnamese universities should advocate at COPE and journal editor forums for explicit permission of AI-assisted language editing, framed as an equity and access issue. This is politically leverageable.
weaknesses_of_this_position: Weakness 1: The position might overstate the equivalence between AI-assisted editing and professional editing. Professional editors provide discipline-specific knowledge (understanding of scientific conventions, terminology, etc.). AI tools (as of 2025) are general-purpose and may not understand scientific nuance. A professional editor would catch a phrase that is grammatically correct but scientifically misleading. AI might not. The position should qualify: 'AI is equivalent to professional editing for language clarity, not for scientific accuracy-checking.' Weakness 2: The position assumes that permitting AI language assistance will not lead to abuse (researchers using AI to generate scientific content, not just edit language). There is a slippery slope risk. The position should be more explicit: 'Permission for AI language editing does NOT extend to AI-generated data, methods, results, or conclusions. Scientific content must be researcher-generated and verified. Only presentation language can be AI-assisted.' Weakness 3: The position assumes the English-language publishing system will continue to be dominant. If publishing becomes more multilingual (through AI translation, open-access journals in multiple languages, etc.), the language barrier problem could decrease. The position should acknowledge: 'This argument is contingent on English remaining the lingua franca of research. If publishing becomes more multilingual, the argument weakens.' Weakness 4: The position might be too quick to accept the status quo of English dominance. A stronger position would demand: 'In addition to permitting AI language assistance for current researchers, fund efforts to create high-quality research publishing in Vietnamese, Mandarin, Spanish, Arabic, etc.' The position should combine pragmatic acceptance (permit AI now) with longer-term structural change (support multilingual publishing). Weakness 5: The position might underestimate the difficulty of distinguishing legitimate AI-assisted language editing from illegitimate AI-generated content. If ChatGPT rewrites a paragraph, did it 'assist' the researcher's language or 'generate' new scientific content? This boundary is contested and hard to enforce. The position should propose: 'Researchers should be explicit about which sentences/paragraphs were substantially AI-edited, and provide a marked version alongside the clean version for verification.' Weakness 6: The position might overstate the harm of current COPE guidance. COPE actually permits AI-assisted language editing; the problem is vagueness of implementation. The position should focus on pushing journals to be clearer about permitting language assistance, rather than suggesting COPE is hostile to non-native researchers.
what_would_change_their_mind: 1. COPE issues explicit guidance (by mid-2026): 'AI-assisted language editing (including grammar, vocabulary, phrasing, tone, and paragraph restructuring) is considered acceptable research practice. It should be disclosed briefly ('This manuscript received AI-assisted English editing') and is not grounds for rejection or extra scrutiny.' If this guidance is published, the position would say 'victory achieved.' 2. Research showing that permitting AI language assistance increases international publication rates from non-Anglophone researchers by 15-25% without increasing fraud/retraction rates. If the evidence shows benefit without harm, journals will follow. 3. Multilingual AI translation becomes sufficiently high-quality (90%+ accuracy for academic/technical text) that researchers can write in Vietnamese and publish in Vietnamese-to-English translated version with no loss of meaning. If this happens, the English barrier could be partially removed. 4. Development of discipline-specific AI tools for research writing (not just general language, but understanding of methods, results formatting, literature review synthesis). If AI tools become sophisticated enough to handle scientific nuance, the equivalence to professional editing becomes stronger. 5. Research showing that non-native researcher publication bias (lower acceptance rates for equivalent quality) is significantly reduced by AI-assisted language editing. If AI can actually solve the language bias problem, journals should explicitly encourage its use. 6. Policy from MOET / Vietnamese universities / Vietnamese research organizations pushing back on COPE/journals: 'We acknowledge AI-assisted language editing as legitimate for Vietnamese researchers and recommend its use. We expect journals to treat AI-edited manuscripts from non-native researchers equally with native-speaker manuscripts.' If Vietnamese authorities take this position, it legitimizes the argument. 7. Accessibility data showing that researchers using AI language assistance publish 20-30% more papers, spend less time on writing, and report higher career satisfaction. If AI increases research productivity overall, the case for permitting it becomes stronger.
